ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Tulsa, OK
ut.description: UT thickness surveys and ultrasonic weld inspection at Tulsa refineries, pipelines, tanks and fab yards. Technicians mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Tulsa, Oklahoma
ut.html:
Atlantis performs ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection (UT) at Tulsa-area refineries, pipeline and compressor facilities, tank farms, fabrication yards and power plants. Scopes range from thickness surveys at condition monitoring locations to angle-beam examination of piping and structural welds. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send isometrics, materials and access details through the UT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic inspection is used around Tulsa

Tulsa grew up on oil and still carries the infrastructure. Refineries sit along the Arkansas River, and pipeline and midstream operators run gathering lines, compressor stations, pump stations and storage terminals across northeast Oklahoma. Every one of those assets has carbon steel walls that corrode and erode, and UT thickness readings at fixed locations are how owners watch that loss between turnarounds.

The second cluster is manufacturing and fabrication. The Tulsa Port of Catoosa sits at the head of the McClellan-Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System, and the industrial park around it hosts steel fabrication and process-equipment manufacturing, with barges delivering plate and heavy components. Weld examination on pressure vessels, skids and structural steel is common work there. Add boilers and heat exchangers in hospitals, universities and processing plants, and storage tanks of every size, and UT touches most of the region's steel.

What UT finds in Oklahoma steel, and what it misses

An ultrasonic probe sends a pulse of sound into the metal and the instrument displays the echoes. Timing the back-wall echo gives remaining wall thickness. Angle-beam shear waves directed into a weld at 45, 60 or 70 degrees reflect from lack of fusion, cracks and slag, so UT can find flaws that sit deep inside a joint where surface methods cannot.

The method has boundaries. Heavy scale, pitting and rough coatings hurt coupling, and a corroded surface can scatter the sound so badly that a reading is lost. Cast and some austenitic weld structures are coarse-grained and hard to interpret. A planar flaw lying parallel to the beam may go unseen, which is why scan plans use more than one angle and both sides of the weld where access allows. Under insulation and in cold or hot service, the technician has to match probe, couplant and procedure to the conditions, and a peak on the screen is evidence to interpret, not a diagnosis.

Codes and Oklahoma's inspection framework

Examination follows ASME Section V: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials and Article 23 for the thickness practice in SE-797. Acceptance comes from the governing code. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 12 for ultrasonic weld examination, and process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.6 and the criteria in Table 341.3.2. Structural steel follows AWS D1.1 and its ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds.

Oklahoma regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Department of Labor. According to the department, boilers are inspected at least yearly by the state or an authorized insurance company, high-pressure boilers twice a year, and some pressure vessels every three years, with inspectors commissioned by the National Board. Interstate pipelines fall under PHMSA, 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, with API 1104 incorporated by reference. Plants covered by OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), must inspect to recognized good engineering practice. See the Oklahoma inspection services hub for the statewide view.

Thickness surveys on refinery and midstream piping

A survey starts with the owner's isometrics and the list of condition monitoring locations. The technician calibrates on a step block of the same material, verifies zero, and reads each CML on a marked grid so the next campaign repeats the exact spot. Dual-element probes handle corroded surfaces, and the A-scan is observed instead of trusting a bare digital number, because pit echoes and doubling can fool a gauge on thin or damaged wall.

Hot piping is routine in refinery service, so high-temperature probes and couplant are selected and readings corrected for temperature. Insulated lines are examined at insulation windows cut by the owner's crew, and the windows are logged so they can be resealed. Injection points, dead legs, elbows downstream of control valves and low points get extra readings because those are where damage concentrates. The Article 5 explainer describes the method behind the survey.

Pipeline digs, tank shells and weld examination

Midstream owners compare in-line inspection results with direct measurement at excavated locations. UT at an integrity dig confirms remaining wall at the anomaly and checks the surrounding pipe for laminations that an in-line tool may have reported ambiguously. The data goes back to the operator's integrity engineer, who decides on repair or recoat under the operator's program and PHMSA rules.

Aboveground tanks are surveyed for shell thickness at courses and nozzles, with readings referenced to the owner's API 653 program. For weld work, the technician builds a distance-amplitude reference from side-drilled holes, scans from both sides, and evaluates indications against the table the code names. ASTM E164 covers contact ultrasonic examination of weldments and ASTM E114 covers straight-beam work on plate and forgings. Atlantis performs the NDE and reports the data; the owner's inspector of record signs the API report.

Damage mechanisms that set the survey plan

Refinery owners organize inspection around the damage the process causes, and API 571 lists the mechanisms. Overhead systems on crude units can thin from acidic condensate, high-temperature sulfur service attacks carbon steel in hot lines, and corrosion under insulation hides in cold and cyclic services where water gets trapped. Erosion shows up at elbows, tees and downstream of control valves, and fatigue and vibration cracking appear on small-bore connections.

Midstream assets have their own pattern. Compressor stations see pulsation and vibration on small-bore piping, liquids terminals see bottom-water corrosion at tank floors, and buried pipe sees external corrosion where coating has failed. Because the plan follows the mechanism, the owner's damage-mechanism review is one of the first documents a Tulsa crew asks to see.

Calibration, couplant and the errors UT is prone to

Most UT errors come from setup. A probe calibrated on the wrong material, a zero that drifted after the probe wore, or couplant that burned off a hot surface can all give a plausible but wrong number. Technicians verify calibration at the start, at intervals during the shift and at the end, and re-check after any change of probe, cable or instrument setting. Surface roughness, curvature and coating thickness are accounted for, and any reading taken outside the calibrated range is flagged.

Weld examination adds its own pitfalls: geometric reflectors at the root and cap, spurious echoes from mode conversion and the difficulty of sizing a flaw by amplitude alone. A competent Level II recognizes these, repeats the scan from another direction and, where the procedure demands it, records what could not be examined rather than implying full coverage. Coverage limits are written into the report.

Who performs and reviews the work

Technicians are qualified under the company written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II calibrates, performs and interprets the examination, while an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report before release. Anoop Rayavarapu, the founder, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Certification of each technician is issued by the employer under its written practice, and customers can ask to see qualification records before mobilization.

Owners who want their own procedures or written practice built or updated can use Level III consulting and written practice development.

What a Tulsa UT report contains

  • Line, vessel or tank identification, the isometric or drawing reference, material and nominal wall.
  • Procedure number and revision, code and edition, and the acceptance criteria applied to weld indications.
  • Instrument, probes, couplant and calibration blocks, with calibration checks recorded through the shift.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III who reviewed the package.
  • A CML table showing each reading, the prior reading if supplied, and the loss between campaigns.
  • Weld indications located by position, length, depth and amplitude, with sketches and an accept or reject call.

The report has to work for three readers: the owner, whoever repairs the equipment, and the commissioned inspector who signs off. Under Oklahoma rules, repairs to boilers and pressure vessels are done by firms certified by the Department of Labor, so readings, minimums and procedure revisions are laid out to travel with the repair package.

Planning a UT job around Tulsa

Oklahoma weather decides a lot. Summer sun can heat steel past what ordinary couplant tolerates by mid-morning, spring storms and wind interrupt outdoor work on tank shells and pipe racks, and winter ice storms shut access roads. Refinery turnarounds in the region cluster in spring and fall, so shutdown scopes should be booked ahead of the season. Gathering and compressor sites are often remote, which lengthens travel and calls for early notice of access and gate requirements.

Site entry matters as much as the technique. Refineries and gas plants need orientation, hot-work and confined-space permits, and sometimes gas monitoring. Tell us operating temperatures, insulation type, scaffold needs and who supplies lifts. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa; crews are mobilized to the site, and arrival is confirmed when the scope, permits and travel are settled.

Specifying a Tulsa UT scope that avoids rework

Most scope disputes come from vague wording. A good request names the line or tank, the number of CMLs, the grid at each location, whether insulation windows are provided, what minimum wall is relevant and which code edition governs. For weld work it names the joint type, thickness range, scan coverage required and the acceptance table. Spelling that out lets the crew bring the right probes and block set and keeps the report aligned with what the owner's inspector expects.

UT, MT or PT for your Tulsa job

Choose UT for wall thickness and for flaws inside a weld. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Tulsa for surface cracks on carbon and low-alloy steel, and liquid penetrant testing in Tulsa for stainless and other non-magnetic alloys. A typical repair uses all three: UT to measure what remains, MT or PT on the excavation, and UT on the repair weld afterward. The national ultrasonic testing page describes the method in general.

Training your own UT technicians

Tulsa employers training new inspectors can use UT Level 2 and UT Level 1, with online theory and a practical finished with an ASNT Level III. The UT simulator gives trainees calibration and scanning practice. See NDT training in Tulsa for the full options.

faq.q: What does a Tulsa ultrasonic thickness survey need before it can be quoted?
faq.a: Isometrics or CML drawings, material and nominal wall, operating temperature, insulation and coating, the last campaign's readings, the governing code, site access rules and the dates of any planned outage.

faq.q: Can UT be done on hot refinery piping around Tulsa?
faq.a: Yes, within limits. High-temperature probes and couplant are selected for the surface temperature and readings are corrected for the effect of heat on sound velocity. Extremely hot lines may be better surveyed during a shutdown.

faq.q: Does UT replace radiography on pipeline girth welds?
faq.a: Only where the operator's specification and API 1104 permit it. The substitution, and the acceptance criteria that go with it, must be agreed with the operator and the engineer before the work starts.

faq.q: Who signs the API 653 or API 510 report after UT data is collected?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector signs. Atlantis performs the nondestructive examination and reports the data, including thickness at CMLs, without acting as inspector of record under the API codes.

faq.q: How does Oklahoma regulate boiler and pressure vessel inspection?
faq.a: The Oklahoma Department of Labor runs the program. Boilers are inspected at least yearly, high-pressure boilers twice yearly, and some vessels every three years, by inspectors commissioned by the National Board.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Tulsa office or lab?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa. Technicians are mobilized to your refinery, plant, yard or pipeline site for the agreed scope, with an ASNT Level III reviewing procedures and reports.

faq.q: What happens if UT finds a reading below the stated minimum?
faq.a: The reading is flagged to your inspector during the job and recorded in the report. Decisions on repair, re-rating or continued service stay with the owner and the inspector responsible under the governing code.

faq.q: Can UT find corrosion under insulation near Tulsa?
faq.a: UT measures the wall where the insulation has been opened. It does not see through insulation, so owners cut windows at likely spots, and Atlantis records each window so the insulation can be properly resealed.

faq.q: Can Tulsa technicians train in UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 theory is delivered online and the practical is completed with an ASNT Level III. The employer issues certification under its written practice once experience hours are documented.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Tulsa, OK | MT Testing
mt.description: Mag particle testing of welds, vessels, forgings and structural steel at Tulsa refineries, pipeline facilities and fab yards. Mobilized to site. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Tulsa, Oklahoma
mt.html:
Atlantis performs magnetic particle inspection (MT) on welds, forgings and structural steel at Tulsa refineries, pipeline facilities, tank farms and fabrication yards. MT finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel quickly and clearly. Technicians travel to your site, follow a written procedure and report each indication against the code. Send your component list and access details through the MT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used around Tulsa

Tulsa's oil and gas heritage means a lot of carbon steel under stress. Refinery pressure vessels, heat exchanger shells, piping repairs and structural pipe racks all pass through MT after welding or grinding. Midstream operators examine valve bodies, flange welds, pig-launcher fittings and compressor station piping, and fabricators at the Port of Catoosa industrial park build skids, vessels and structural assemblies that need weld examination before shipment.

Smaller repair jobs are just as common. A crack ground out of a weld needs MT on the excavation before welding and again on the finished surface. Lifting lugs and pad eyes on equipment that will be moved by crane are examined before the pick. Rotating equipment, shafts and flanges in the region's plants are examined at turnaround for service-induced cracking. Because most of this steel is ferromagnetic, MT is quick and cost-effective compared with other surface methods.

What MT finds, and what it misses

MT magnetizes a part and applies iron particles. A crack or seam that interrupts the field leaks flux, the particles gather there, and a visible line forms. The method finds cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and lack of fusion that break the surface or lie just beneath it, and it is very sensitive to tight cracks that penetrant liquid might struggle to enter.

Limits matter in a plant that also contains stainless and alloy piping. MT works only on ferromagnetic materials: carbon and low-alloy steels, not austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or most nickel alloys. It does not find deep internal flaws or measure thickness, and the field must cross the flaw at a useful angle, so two examinations at right angles are required. Thick coatings reduce sensitivity, and weld spatter or heavy scale create false indications that have to be cleaned away.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Tulsa MT work

The method follows ASME Section V Article 7, with ASTM E709 as the guide and ASTM E1444 as a common practice standard. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 6 for MT method and acceptance, and process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2. Structural work follows AWS D1.1, and the Article 7 explainer describes the method requirements in plain terms.

For pressure equipment in Oklahoma, the Department of Labor oversees boilers and pressure vessels, and repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. Only firms certified by the department may install, service or repair this equipment in the state, so MT results usually travel inside a repair package that a commissioned inspector will review. Pipeline owners work to PHMSA rules, 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, with API 1104 for welding. The Oklahoma inspection services page lists the statewide picture.

Technique: yokes, prods, coils and carriers

Field MT is mostly done with an electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke must show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the pole spacing in use, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, proven with a calibrated test weight at the start of the shift. Prods inject current into heavy sections but can arc-burn the surface, so many owners restrict them on vessels in service.

Dry powder, applied in a light cloud, suits rough welds and warm surfaces and is easy to use outdoors. Wet visible and wet fluorescent suspensions are more sensitive; fluorescent work needs a darkened area and UV-A light at the intensity set by the procedure. Field indicators confirm field direction and strength. After the examination, parts going to machining, welding or sensitive service are demagnetized and the residual field is checked.

Typical discontinuities in refinery and midstream steel

The technician looks for the damage the service is likely to cause. Hardenable steels welded without enough preheat show hydrogen cracking in the heat-affected zone. Wet hydrogen sulfide service can produce cracking at weld toes in vessels and piping. Fatigue cracks start at stress concentrations: branch connections, support attachments, small-bore connections that vibrate, and the toes of fillet welds on structural supports.

At turnaround, MT is frequently called for on selected welds in vessels and on nozzle attachments, with the extent set by the owner's inspection plan. It is also used on lifting equipment and rigging hardware, and on structural welds where load testing is not an option. Recording the location and orientation of each indication matters, because trend and sizing decisions later depend on it.

Surface preparation, lighting and system checks

An MT result is only as reliable as the surface and the setup behind it. Loose scale, paint, oil and weld spatter in the examination zone are removed and the surface is dried. Under visible light the part must reach the illumination the procedure states, read with a light meter, and for fluorescent work the UV-A intensity at the surface and the ambient white light are both measured and written down.

Wet systems get a settling test for particle concentration and a check on a reference part, and the yoke lifting test is repeated if the equipment is moved or the pole spacing changes. In a refinery these checks also protect against false negatives from a weak field. They are listed in the report so a reviewer can see the examination was properly controlled.

Repair excavations and welding on hardenable steel

One routine MT job around Tulsa is proving a crack removal. After a defect is ground out of a pressure part, MT on the excavation confirms nothing remains before welding, and a second examination after the finished weld and grinding closes the loop. On hardenable steels MT is often repeated after a delay, since hydrogen cracking can appear hours after welding. The owner's inspection plan sets the hold time and the extent.

The same approach applies to temporary attachments removed from vessels and to repairs on structural supports. One report that records the excavation, the repair and the final surface gives the owner and the commissioned inspector a clean chain of evidence, which matters when an Oklahoma-certified repair firm hands the package back to the owner.

Who performs and reviews the work

A Level II technician qualified under the Atlantis written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications. A Level III signs off the procedure and reviews the report before it is released. That Level III role is filled by the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Certification records, vision examinations and training history are available to customers on request, since the employer issues certification under SNT-TC-1A.

If your own procedure needs checking against ASME Section V, or a new MT procedure must be written for a vessel or pipeline facility, Level III consulting can take that on.

What a Tulsa MT report contains

  • Part, weld or vessel identification, drawing reference, material and surface condition.
  • Procedure number and revision, code and edition, and the acceptance standard that applies.
  • Technique: yoke, prods or coil, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent, and the particle product used.
  • Equipment checks including the yoke lifting test, light meter readings and particle concentration.
  • Each indication by location, orientation and length, with a sketch or photograph and an accept or reject call.
  • Whether demagnetization was done, with the residual field reading, plus the names and levels of the Level II and the reviewing Level III.

Atlantis reports relevant and non-relevant indications separately. The owner's inspector decides disposition, and repair work in Oklahoma is carried out by a firm the Department of Labor has certified.

Planning an MT job around Tulsa

Oklahoma heat is the biggest planning factor. Steel standing in summer sun is far too hot for some liquid carriers, dry powder behaves differently on very warm surfaces, and fluorescent work in daylight needs shade or a blackout enclosure. Winter ice storms and cold mornings complicate access and slow handling. Spring thunderstorms and wind can pause outdoor work on tank shells and pipe racks without warning.

Turnaround schedules drive demand, so MT scopes are best booked before the spring and fall windows. Refineries and gas plants require safety orientation, hot-work coordination and sometimes gas monitoring. Surface preparation, especially coating removal and grinding of weld caps, should be included in the scope and the schedule. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa, so crews travel to the site with equipment and the arrival plan is agreed when the job is quoted.

Lifting hardware, rigging and structural attachments

Tulsa's fabricators and plants lift heavy equipment constantly, so lugs, shackles, hooks and spreader beams are common MT subjects. The examination looks for fatigue cracks at weld toes and at the root of threads, and for cracks that start at corrosion pits. Findings are recorded with a sketch and the part is tagged by its owner. MT is also used on structural attachments to vessels and pipe racks before and after load events such as high wind.

MT, PT or UT for your Tulsa job

MT is the quickest, most sensitive surface check on carbon and low-alloy steel. For stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals, use dye penetrant inspection in Tulsa. For wall thickness or flaws inside a weld, use ultrasonic testing in Tulsa. The national magnetic particle testing page covers the method in general, and the MT complete guide goes deeper.

Training your own MT technicians

Tulsa employers can train inspectors through MT Level 1 and MT Level 2, with online theory and a practical completed with an ASNT Level III. The NDT training in Tulsa page lists the options, and the practice tests help candidates prepare for the written exams.

faq.q: What Tulsa equipment is usually inspected with MT?
faq.a: Carbon and low-alloy steel items: pressure vessel and piping welds, nozzle attachments, valve and flange welds, lifting lugs, structural supports, shafts and repair excavations. Stainless and aluminum items need penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: Is MT or PT better for weld repairs in a Tulsa refinery?
faq.a: On carbon steel MT is usually preferred because it is more sensitive and also finds slightly subsurface cracks. On stainless or alloy steel PT is the correct method because those materials are not magnetic.

faq.q: Can MT be done on hot surfaces in Oklahoma summers?
faq.a: Dry powder can be used on warmer surfaces than wet suspensions, but every technique has a temperature limit in its procedure. If the steel is hotter than the limit, the work is scheduled for a cooler time or the procedure is qualified at the higher temperature.

faq.q: Why must MT be applied in two directions?
faq.a: Cracks are revealed only when the field crosses them at a useful angle. ASME Section V requires two examinations at roughly right angles so that discontinuities running in any direction are detected.

faq.q: Does MT find cracks under paint?
faq.a: A thin coating of limited thickness may be tolerated if the technique is demonstrated for it, but heavy paint or scale reduces sensitivity. The procedure states the allowable coating thickness, and otherwise the coating is removed at the test zone.

faq.q: Who reviews the MT report before it reaches me?
faq.a: An ASNT Level III reviews the report before release. The Level II technician who did the examination is named in the record along with the procedure, equipment checks and every indication found.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or crew in Tulsa?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the scope, and the arrival arrangements are confirmed when the job is quoted with you.

faq.q: What does an MT quote request need?
faq.a: A list of components or welds, materials, surface condition and coating, access and elevation, the code and edition, whether fluorescent or visible particles are required, dates, and any site orientation or permit rules.

faq.q: How is MT used at turnaround in Oklahoma plants?
faq.a: Owners specify selected welds, nozzle attachments and lifting hardware in the inspection plan. MT is done after cleaning, and any indications are located, recorded and passed to the owner's inspector for disposition.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Tulsa, OK | Liquid PT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection of stainless, alloy and aluminum welds at Tulsa refineries, plants and shops. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Tulsa, Oklahoma
pt.html:
Atlantis performs liquid penetrant testing (PT), also called dye penetrant inspection, on stainless and alloy welds, castings and machined parts at Tulsa refineries, chemical and processing plants and fabrication shops. PT finds surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps on any clean, non-porous metal. Technicians travel to your site. Tell us the material, surface finish and governing code in the PT quote form; a reply comes within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used around Tulsa

Stainless and alloy steel are everywhere in Tulsa's process industries. Refinery heat exchangers, alloy piping, reactor internals and stainless tubing all need a surface examination that does not rely on magnetism, and PT is the standard answer. Tubesheet welds, socket welds, branch connections and instrument connections are typical locations. Fabricators at the Port of Catoosa industrial park also build stainless and alloy process equipment where PT is called for before shipment.

Repair excavations are another daily use. After a crack is ground out, PT on the excavation proves it is gone before welding, and the finished weld is examined again. Machined and cast components from regional manufacturers, along with aluminum fittings and other non-ferrous parts, are tested by PT as well. In the field, solvent-removable visible dye is the usual workhorse because it needs no water supply and no blackout enclosure.

What PT finds, and what it misses

PT uses capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid applied to a clean surface is drawn into any opening that reaches the surface, and after excess is removed a developer pulls it back out and makes the opening visible. Cracks, laps, seams, porosity and incomplete fusion that break the surface appear as bleed-out lines or dots, with sharp contrast in white light or under UV-A for fluorescent systems.

It cannot see below the surface. Internal voids, buried lack of fusion and cracks sealed by peening or machining smear will not show. Contaminants such as oil, paint, rust and weld flux block the openings and must be removed. Rough or porous surfaces hold penetrant and produce background that hides small indications. For the full-thickness question, ultrasonic testing is the better tool, and for carbon steel where a yoke fits, magnetic particle inspection is often more sensitive.

Codes, materials and acceptance criteria

The method is written to ASME Section V Article 6, supported by ASTM E165. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 8, which treats only indications larger than 1/16 inch as relevant and sets limits on linear and rounded indications. Process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 and stainless fabrication under AWS D1.6 accept PT where the contract calls for it.

Materials need attention on alloy work. Article 6 limits sulfur and halogen content in penetrant materials used on nickel-base alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium, so batch numbers are recorded for cleaner, penetrant and developer. Oklahoma allows only firms certified by the Department of Labor to install, service or repair boilers and pressure vessels, and inspectors must hold National Board commissions, so PT on a repair becomes part of a package that a commissioned inspector reviews. The Article 6 explainer covers the method requirements in detail.

Technique: from precleaning to inspection

The sequence is fixed by the procedure. The surface is cleaned and dried, penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion, and it dwells for the stated time. Excess is removed by solvent wipe, water wash or emulsifier depending on the method, developer is applied in a thin even coat, and the surface is examined after the development time.

Penetrants are classed by type and method. Type I is fluorescent, examined in a darkened area under UV-A light, and Type II is visible dye viewed in white light. Method A is water-washable, Methods B and D use emulsifiers, and Method C is solvent-removable. Field work around Tulsa is mostly Type II, Method C because it needs no water and no darkness. Shop work on machined and cast parts more often uses fluorescent systems for higher sensitivity. Postcleaning removes residue where parts return to service.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

A mark on the developer is not automatically a defect. A relevant indication is caused by a real discontinuity and is judged against the acceptance table. A non-relevant indication comes from part geometry, such as a thread root, a sharp edge or a press fit. A false indication comes from handling or poor cleaning. Separating them is exactly what a Level II is certified to do.

When an indication is uncertain, the technician wipes it away, reapplies developer and watches whether it returns in the same place and shape. Rounded and linear indications are measured separately because the acceptance tables treat them differently, and the report records which criteria were applied. That detail lets the owner's inspector check the call instead of taking it on trust.

Common ways penetrant jobs go wrong

Poor results usually start with preparation. Grinding, blasting or wire brushing can smear metal across the openings that PT is supposed to find, so ground and machined parts often need etching or careful mechanical cleaning first. Residual oil, paint, rust or weld flux blocks entry, too much developer can mask small indications, and an over-aggressive wash can pull penetrant out of real cracks and leave a falsely clean part.

Timing and temperature cause the next group of errors. Too short a dwell may not let penetrant reach tight cracks, while developer left too long bleeds and blurs. Temperature outside the qualified range changes viscosity and evaporation. The procedure fixes each control, and the technician logs them so the owner can verify the process followed the document.

Heat exchangers, tubesheets and small-bore connections

Refinery and gas plant exchangers produce a steady stream of PT work. After retubing or seal-weld repairs, tube-to-tubesheet welds are examined for cracks and pinholes, often with fluorescent penetrant where the geometry allows. Socket welds, instrument taps and branch connections on small-bore piping are examined the same way when MT cannot reach. The technician records each joint by its position so a later reviewer can find it again.

Who performs and reviews the work

A Level II technician, qualified under the Atlantis written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, carries out and interprets each penetrant examination. The procedure, with its dwell times, temperature range and material controls, is approved by an ASNT Level III, who also reviews the report. At the top of that chain is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Near-vision and color-contrast checks are required of technicians under the written practice, since the whole method depends on seeing faint indications.

If you need a PT procedure for alloy piping or a repair program, Level III consulting and written practice development are available as separate services.

What a Tulsa PT report contains

  • Component, weld or part identification, material and surface finish, and the area examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, code edition and the acceptance standard.
  • Penetrant type, method, sensitivity level and manufacturer, with batch numbers for cleaner, penetrant and developer.
  • Surface temperature, dwell and development times, and light measurements.
  • Every indication with location, size, shape and rounded or linear classification, plus an accept or reject call.
  • Postcleaning performed, and the technician and reviewing Level III by name and level.

Atlantis supplies the examination and its record. Acceptance and any repair decision remain with the owner and the commissioned inspector.

Matching the scope to the specification

A penetrant scope holds up at review when it names the penetrant type and method, the sensitivity level, the acceptance standard and the temperature range. Aerospace-style parts and some fabricated components follow ASTM E1417 and the customer's own specification, while plant repairs usually follow the construction code. Settling this before mobilization avoids procedures being rewritten on site, and it tells the Level III what to approve.

Planning a PT job around Tulsa

The standard technique in ASME Section V Article 6 covers 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Summer sun on tank shells and pipe racks can push steel past the upper limit by mid-morning, and winter mornings fall below freezing. Crews measure surface temperature before applying penetrant, work in shade or under cover, and shift the work to cooler or warmer hours, or use a qualified non-standard technique, when neither is practical.

Wind and dust in spring storm season affect developer application outdoors, and rain stops the work. Refinery entry requires orientation and hot-work coordination, and chemical-free alternatives or approved cleaners may be required by the plant. Surface preparation, including removing coatings and heat tint, should be written into the scope. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa, so travel and arrival are arranged with you when the job is quoted.

Alloy materials and contamination control

Alloy work needs more discipline than carbon steel. Cleaners and penetrants that carry chlorine or sulfur can harm austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, so only approved material batches are used and containers are labeled. Wipes, brushes and gloves are kept clean and dedicated to the alloy, and carbon steel dust from a neighboring job is kept away from stainless surfaces. These controls are routine in a well-run penetrant job, and the report names the products so the owner can confirm compliance.

Postcleaning is just as important. Developer and penetrant residue left in crevices can interfere with later welding or service, so parts are cleaned to the owner's requirement before they are released, and the cleaning is recorded as a step in the report.

PT, MT or UT for your Tulsa job

Use PT for stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic alloys, and for small or awkward welds on any material. Use magnetic particle inspection in Tulsa for carbon and low-alloy steel where it is more sensitive. Use ultrasonic testing in Tulsa for thickness or flaws inside a weld. The national penetrant testing page covers the method in general and the MT versus PT guide helps with borderline cases.

Training your own PT technicians

PT is a good first method for new inspectors. PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 use online theory with a practical completed with an ASNT Level III, and the PT simulator gives repetitions on dwell, removal and interpretation. See NDT training in Tulsa for the options.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing find on Tulsa refinery alloy piping?
faq.a: Surface-breaking cracks, porosity, laps and incomplete fusion in welds, tubesheet joints and branch connections. It cannot see flaws below the surface, so internal conditions require ultrasonic or another volumetric method.

faq.q: Which penetrant system is common in Oklahoma field work?
faq.a: Type II visible dye with Method C solvent removal is the usual field choice, because it needs no water supply and no darkened enclosure. Shop work on machined parts often uses fluorescent systems for sensitivity.

faq.q: What temperature limits does PT have in Oklahoma summers?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Hot steel in sun can exceed that, so crews measure temperature, shade the work or use a qualified technique.

faq.q: Why are batch numbers recorded for penetrant materials?
faq.a: Article 6 limits sulfur and halogen content for materials used on nickel-base alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium. Batch numbers let the owner show that compliant materials were used on the job.

faq.q: Can PT be used instead of MT on carbon steel?
faq.a: Yes, PT works on any clean non-porous metal. MT is generally more sensitive on carbon steel and finds slightly subsurface flaws, but PT is useful where a yoke cannot reach or where the surface is too finished for MT.

faq.q: What counts as a rejectable indication under ASME Section VIII Appendix 8?
faq.a: Only indications larger than 1/16 inch are relevant. Any relevant linear indication is rejected, and rounded indications are limited by size and spacing. The report records which criteria were applied.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Tulsa?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, shop or yard for the scope, and an ASNT Level III reviews the procedure and the report.

faq.q: What do you need for a PT quote in Tulsa?
faq.a: A list of welds or parts, material and finish, coatings or heat tint to remove, the code and edition, whether fluorescent or visible penetrant is required, temperature conditions, access and site safety requirements.

faq.q: Who issues PT certification for my technicians?
faq.a: The employer does, as SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based system run through the company's own written practice. PT Level 1 and Level 2 training from Atlantis supports that, and the employer decides when its people qualify.

rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. Tulsa options: UT, ASNT Level III review of radiographs, and RT theory training. Request a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Tulsa, Oklahoma
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, and that includes Tulsa. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity: the sources and X-ray equipment are regulated under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules in 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of the state where the work happens. It is not a service Atlantis offers here. This page sets out what a Tulsa owner can get from Atlantis if a specification or a search pointed to radiography.

Why Tulsa owners ask for radiography

Pipeline girth welds, refinery piping, pressure vessels and steel castings are often specified with radiographic examination, because an image gives a permanent record of volumetric flaws. Foundry buyers also grade castings against ASTM reference radiographs, and operators of gas and liquids lines call for RT on new construction. When the contract demands RT, the owner engages a licensed radiography contractor, and the licence holder, exposure plan and safety zone are that contractor's responsibility. Atlantis does not name or recommend one.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative

Where the construction code and the owner allow, UT examines the full thickness of a weld without a radiation source. Paragraphs of ASME B31.3 and of API 1104 allow ultrasonic examination of production welds, and AWS D1.1 sets separate acceptance rules for ultrasonic work on groove welds. ASME Section VIII lets ultrasonic stand in for radiography under certain conditions only. Whoever proposes the substitution has to agree it with the owner, the engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector before the work begins. Ultrasonic testing in Tulsa describes how that examination is performed.

ASNT Level III radiography review without a radiation licence

Reviewing radiography needs no source. An ASNT Level III can check radiographs, whether film or digital images, and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical engagements are a second read on disputed indications, an independent look at image quality, coverage and identification, and a review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice before the work starts. The reviewer is the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, who is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. See Level III consulting and written practice development.

Radiographic testing theory for your team

Employers building a radiography group can train technicians in theory through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Hands-on exposure work happens under the licence of the employer or contractor and is separate from this training. The NDT training in Tulsa page lists local options, and the MT and PT pages describe the surface methods that Atlantis does carry out around Tulsa. The Oklahoma inspection services page gives the statewide picture.

Send a Tulsa review request with the radiographs or image files, the technique sheet, the code and edition the work was built to, and the acceptance criteria in the contract. With those in hand, the Level III can usually judge whether the images support the stated result and whether coverage and image quality meet Article 2. The outcome is a written review for your engineer or inspector to file with the project records.

How to start

If you need UT, MT or PT in Tulsa, or a Level III review of another contractor's radiographs, send the specification and the examination you need through the quote form. Atlantis has no office in Tulsa, so technicians are mobilized to your site for any on-site scope, and review work can often be done from the records. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do radiography in Tulsa?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States because the work is licensed under NRC or state rules. Ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant inspection are available, along with Level III review of radiographs.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace RT on a pipeline weld near Tulsa?
faq.a: Only where the operator's specification and the code allow it. API 1104 and ASME B31.3 contain ultrasonic provisions, and the substitution has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can a Level III review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and can give a second read on disputed indications.

faq.q: Does Atlantis train people in radiographic testing?
faq.a: Radiographic testing Level 2 theory can be taken through Atlantis. Hands-on exposure work is done under the licence of the employer or contractor, and certification comes from the employer under its written practice.

faq.q: Who handles radiography licensing in Oklahoma?
faq.a: The licence holder, normally the radiography contractor, confirms whether the NRC or the state agency regulates the work. Atlantis does not name contractors, and this page does not replace advice from the licensing authority.
